research_analysis.exact_observed_hook: First spoken sentence (the off-screen caller, screamed): "STOP CALLING ME!" On-screen text at 0:00: "237th dial of the day" / "Open to constructive criticism".
research_analysis.visual_hook: A young man in glasses, blue dress shirt, tie and an over-ear headset sits in an office chair with his chin on his hand, eyes closed and tired. White wall, drop ceiling and a TV showing a VIZIO logo behind him. A white text box sits over the shot.
research_analysis.narrative_structure: One static take, zero cuts, 16 seconds. 0-3s a calm caption sets an optimistic premise. 4s an off-screen caller explodes. The salesman answers once, calmly, then loses it laughing behind his hand while the caller keeps going. Ends on a text CTA.
research_analysis.viral_mechanism: Contrast between a polite, deadpan caption and audio that immediately contradicts it. The salesman only gets one line, so the viewer watches his face do the work.
research_analysis.observed_evidence: 9.7M views on a 20K-follower account, 142.2x that creator's 68.5K median. Zero cuts. Text appears before any sound. The salesman speaks one sentence in 16 seconds. No music. The walkthrough does not establish whether the call is real or staged.
research_analysis.performance_hypothesis: Hypothesis: the caption makes a promise in the first second (this call will go badly) and the payoff arrives by second 4, so almost nobody leaves before it. People who have worked a phone job send it to a coworker with 'this is us'. Comments are other salespeople posting their own worst call.
research_analysis.why_this_format_fits_alex: Same grammar as his biggest results: one shot, a short text line, a face doing the acting. His 13.5M Central Park Reel is a single-shot face reaction, and this adds the one thing his recent feed lacks, which is his actual job (selling a content agency to local businesses).
research_analysis.originality_changes: Borrowed: single static take, calm caption, a phone voice that derails the call, one calm reply from the seller. New: the prospect does not yell. He is a gym owner who out-sells Alex with Alex's own closing lines, and Alex ends up buying. No profanity, no real call audio, all lines new.

alex_adaptation.concept: Alex cold-calls a gym to pitch content. The owner flips it and runs a hard close on Alex for a gym membership, using the exact pressure lines a salesperson would use. Alex, beaten at his own game, asks if they take Visa.
alex_adaptation.target_audience: People who sell for a living (agency owners, SDRs, realtors, gym staff) and anyone who has been upsold by a gym.
alex_adaptation.primary_emotion: Amused recognition, with second-hand embarrassment for Alex.
alex_adaptation.first_frame: Alex at a desk, phone to his ear, coffee in the other hand, eyebrows up and confident. Text box top-center already on screen: "Cold call #41 today" and under it "Feeling good about this one".
alex_adaptation.first_spoken_line: Hey, is this the owner? It's Alex, I help gyms get a million views on

production.location: Home desk or any plain desk with a wall behind it
production.wardrobe: Button-up shirt, sleeves rolled once. Looks like someone trying to seem professional.
shot_list: One static chest-up take, 18 to 20 seconds, played against the pre-recorded owner lines through an earbud so reactions are timed
Separate audio-only recording of the three owner lines in a brighter, older voice
production.editor_instructions: Record the owner lines first and play them in one earbud while filming so Alex's pauses are real. Apply a telephone EQ (cut below 300 Hz and above 3.4 kHz) to the owner. Owner captions yellow, Alex captions white. Do not add music. Keep the full second of silence before 'Do you take Visa?'.

variants_to_test: Alternate hook: "I teach brands how to sell. Watch this."

testing.promotion_decision: Brand fit 3 (shows him selling the agency). follow_up_variations_if_successful: Cold call #42: a restaurant owner puts Alex on hold and the hold music is the owner singing

creative_confidence.rationale: One take, one location, a clear reversal, and the punchline is four words. The numbered cold-call frame makes it a series. It shows his job without explaining it.
uncertainties: The reference's energy came from an explosive caller; this version trades shock for a status reversal, which is quieter
Alex voicing the owner must sound like a different person or the joke reads as him talking to himself
Whether the reference call was real is unknown, so part of its pull may have been authenticity this staged version does not have
